verdict.tagline: Endless tabletop nights, dragged down by clunky controls.
for_you_if: you want to play board games with distant friends
you rely on community workshop mods for content
not_for_you_if: you need stable performance with heavy workshop assets
you cannot stand a steep learning curve for controls
you expect the virtual reality mode to work well

cohorts.label: 2-20h
cohorts.summary: New players grapple with awkward controls and performance drops from heavy workshop assets.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game's controls take time to learn and get used to.

citations.review_text:
Just played a game of Commander with a mock up of my real life deck. 3 hours later i won. 
I also was using the OG Steam Controller, the weird looking one with 2 round touchpads, and ngl it was a learning curve but worked WONDERS sitting and playing this on a big 65inch 4K screen. Cards looked clean and crisp. 
Sometimes dont have the room to pull out the cards or time to meet in person to play with the real cards. This really helped. 
Oh yeah this is a real cool game that has some cool workshop content. 
totally worth the price. I see games in the workshop i havent seen since i was a child like that pokemon board game in the early 2000s late 90s.
Again all i played was one match of Magic The Gathering Commander 3 way match.

Great!
Controls take some time to get used to.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that loading heavy workshop assets can cause significant performance lag and crashes.

citations.review_text:
The system is good at accommodating to the server needs of your game group.
A grand variety of games, including people making their own games with personalized assets, means literally any game night is available to you.
If you're facing significant lag, it's more likely that you are loading a workshop game that is more than your personal computer's processor can chew. Good news is, you see warning signs of this when the program is loading the assets to your side of the web client. You can use that as a measure of how gently you need to move to avoid a lagging disaster.
I like crashing my game in uno infinity

claims.claim: Reviewers living in the UK experience issues where imgur-related content fails to work within the game.

citations.review_text: Not a recommend on one condition: If you live in the UK. Due to the government being out of touch bellends, anything imgur related will not work, including things in this game. It's not the devs fault.

I’m going to start this by saying that if you want to play a board game with your friends but don’t have the ability to/don’t want to meet up in person then this is practically the only option. At least for playing a variety of board games. However, that does not give Tabletop Simulator a pass for its flaws which I will get into for this review.

But I always start with the positives. Tabletop Simulator is great in concept. An online platform that allows for you to play a variety of board games online with your friends sounds amazing on paper. And it does have the potential to be great in practice. There are online servers if you wish to play an available game over the internet with strangers. Not exactly my cup of tea, but there most definitely is an audience for that sort of thing and I try to be objective. The host does have more power than other players so if someone is just there harming the play experience for everyone else they can be kicked. An amazing part in concept is Tabletop Simulators ability to allow you to create your own custom board games. You can go through and design pretty much anything so long as you have the skill and knowledge to do so. You can even import your own 3D models. However, even this has flaws which I will get into in my next section. The best part though, is definitely the fact Tabletop Simulator has a Steam Workshop. As such all creations can be shared, and you can download the things other people have created.

I do really wish Tabletop simulator was good. That would be amazing. But it's not. First and foremost its monetization strategies are abhorrent. This game has 43 different DLCs. All ranging from $4.99 to $12.99 USD (€4.38 to €11.41 for those who live in Europe.) This is unacceptable. If you wish to play, for example, Unearth, you will have to pay $19.99 for the game itself, then pay $5.99 for the Unearth DLC, then your friend will have to do the same. cohorts.label: 20-100h
cohorts.summary: Experienced users rely on community mods for digital game nights despite clunky interfaces and physics quirks.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the physics-based interactions and control scheme can feel janky, leading to objects like cards or pieces flying around and causing frustration.

citations.review_text:
Tabletop Simulator is not a traditional game, but a physics sandbox. The Gameplay (7/10) is extremely flexible, though physics interactions can occasionally cause chaos with flying cards or knocked-over pieces. The Content Depth (11/10) is virtually endless thanks to the Steam Workshop, where the community provides mods for almost every existing board game. The UI & Controls (6/10) feel dated and carry a steep learning curve due to convoluted hotkeys. Performance and Multiplayer (8/10) are solid and run reliably even on lower-end systems.

➕ Massive, highly active community with thousands of free Workshop mods
➕ Built-in VR support and functional media/tablet player at the virtual table
➕ The ultimate tool for developing and playtesting original game designs
➖ No AI opponents or automated rule checks (players must enforce rules manually, just like at a real table)
➖ The physics-based control scheme can cause noticeable frustration during the first few hours

Controls and physics are janky but this is the premier board game sandbox. Though it will never beat playing board games in person, it is a very important tool for the hobby at large, especially for playtesting.

Great medium for game night when folks can't meet in person and/or you want to play something you don't physically own. It's got some issues for sure, but I'd take at-times spotty connection and janky physics over being completely unable to play Magic and board games with friends online. I haven't tried TTS' competitors so I can't compare them, but I haven't had much reason to switch to their competitors, if that says anything.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game relies heavily on community-made mods via the Steam Workshop to provide access to a wide variety of board games.

citations.review_text:
The game is entirely ran by the modding community pretty much. Not really a negative, but its something to keep in mind.

Your not buying a game when you buy tabletop simulator, your buying thousands if not tens of thousands of different games. Definitely worth the price, as even if you don't like how a specific modder implemented your favourite board/card game, there are probably other versions of it unless it is super niche.

I've recently gotten back into using tabletop simulator to play MTG, and while there are some QOL features missing from the website i used to play MTG on, its definitely way smoother and a less buggy experience. Plus you can always improvise on how to attach equipment/auras, track counters etc.

claims.claim: Reviewers mention that the game serves as a useful platform for long-distance game nights with friends or family living far away.

citations.review_text:
I was one of the original Kickstarta Backers so had this game for a while. Steam told me to do a review.
This is a fun way to play board games digitally.
I have played this with my family who is spread across several countries, with friends I usually play in the physical world when we for some reason can't meet. And in solo.
With the workshop there are many more games, and please do buy the real games also to support the makers of those games.
One downside that is not the fault of the makers of TTS is that many of the games in workshop no longer work due to missing assets and similar the makers in the workshop are not updating them.
A lot of work has gone into this so thanks to the devs for making it a possibility. Its a great way to keep my interest in 40k going and to keep in contact with my friends who live far away.
moved across the country away from my friends, very useful for long distance game nights
Best way to play with my friends across the country!

cohorts.summary: Longtime players continue to battle unintuitive controls and a broken virtual reality mode.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the VR mode is unusable and features terribly designed controls.

citations.review_text:
The best boardgame simulator there is. Sadly best and good are not mutually inclusive. 

This programn has some major issues from 
Horrible performance to somewhat unintuitive controlls.
But you ain't finding anything better, so get this and save yourself the pain of searching.

A big positive though is the fact people can make custom games or just even recreate exsiting games to publish and play for free with the workshop. Ontop of their being javascript support to allow for some basic automation.

PS. It has VR support, but do NOT buy it for that! It is basically unusable and the controls go from unintuitive, to designed by satan itself. It is better of not exsisting as a "possible" way to play.

Pretty good, and afaik the only good simulator for boardgames.
Sadly the performance sucks quite a bit, and the VR mode is straight up unusable, the controls are just... Bad to stay polite.

Aside that, probably  the best way to play Tabletop games with your friends.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the controls as unintuitive, taking time to get used to, and involving a steep learning curve due to manipulating 3D objects with a 2D mouse and screen interface.

citations.review_text:
Really fun, tremendously supported, get mad at your friends about dice, but online. 

 The UI is pretty user unfriendly and takes some getting used to and actions can change from game to game. But if you're okay with some teething issues you'll have a great laugh with friends here.

Overall, a great system for playing card/board games!  The number of user created mods is HUGE!
Not without its quirks though.  For one, controls take some getting used to, as there are a lot of them, and you're manipulating stuff in 3D using a 2D system (screen and mouse), which can be confusing for some.  Also it seems like there's an issue with removing zones?  I played last night as the host, and zones a user created couldn't be deleted - "delete" was grayed out for him, and I didn't even have an option for it.
This is an excellent program for tabletop prototyping, as well as playing games of any sort with friends. Yes it has a bit of a learning curve, but it's so powerful it's worth it.
Tts is a very good physics engine for table top games. its difficult to learn and i don't know if it'll ever be second nature but it works well for creating prototype games.
